{{Short description|Polynomial with a matrix as variable}}
{{distinguish|Polynomial matrix}}

In mathematics, a '''matrix polynomial''' is a polynomial with [[square matrix|square matrices]] as variables. Given an ordinary, scalar-valued polynomial
: <math>P(x) = \sum_{i=0}^n{ a_i x^i} =a_0  + a_1 x+ a_2 x^2 + \cdots + a_n x^n, </math>
this polynomial evaluated at a matrix <math>A</math> is
:<math>P(A) = \sum_{i=0}^n{ a_i A^i} =a_0 I + a_1 A + a_2 A^2 + \cdots + a_n A^n,</math>
where <math>I</math> is the [[identity matrix]].{{sfn|Horn|Johnson|1990|p=36}}

Note that <math>P(A)</math> has the same dimension as <math>A</math>.

A '''matrix polynomial equation''' is an equality between two matrix polynomials, which holds for the specific matrices in question.  A '''matrix polynomial identity''' is a matrix polynomial equation which holds for all matrices ''A'' in a specified [[matrix ring]] ''M<sub>n</sub>''(''R'').

Matrix polynomials are often demonstrated in undergraduate linear algebra classes due to their relevance in showcasing properties of [[linear transformations]] represented as matrices, most notably the [[Cayley–Hamilton theorem]].

The determinant of a matrix polynomial with [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian]] [[Positive-definite matrices|positive-definite]] (semidefinite) coefficients is a polynomial with positive (nonnegative) coefficients.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Friedland|first1=S.|last2=Melman|first2=A.|date=2020|title=A note on Hermitian positive semidefinite matrix polynomials|journal=Linear Algebra and Its Applications|language=en|volume=598|pages=105–109|doi=10.1016/j.laa.2020.03.038}}</ref>

==Characteristic and minimal polynomial==
The [[characteristic polynomial]] of a matrix ''A'' is a scalar-valued polynomial, defined by <math>p_A(t) = \det \left(tI - A\right)</math>. The [[Cayley–Hamilton theorem]] states that if this polynomial is viewed as a matrix polynomial and evaluated at the matrix <math>A</math> itself, the result is the zero matrix: <math>p_A(A) = 0</math>. A polynomial ''annihilates'' <math>A</math> if <math>p(A) = 0</math>; <math>p</math> is also known as an ''[[annihilating polynomial]]''. Thus, the characteristic polynomial is a polynomial which annihilates <math>A</math>. 

There is a unique [[monic polynomial]] of minimal degree which annihilates <math>A</math>; this polynomial is the [[minimal polynomial (linear algebra)|minimal polynomial]]. Any polynomial which annihilates <math>A</math> (such as the characteristic polynomial) is a multiple of the minimal polynomial.{{sfn|Horn|Johnson|1990|loc=Thm 3.3.1}}

It follows that given two polynomials <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math>, we have <math> P(A) = Q(A) </math> if and only if 
:<math> P^{(j)}(\lambda_i) = Q^{(j)}(\lambda_i) \qquad \text{for } j = 0,\ldots,n_i-1 \text{ and } i = 1,\ldots,s, </math>
where <math> P^{(j)} </math> denotes the <math>j</math>th derivative of <math>P</math> and <math> \lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_s </math> are the [[eigenvalue]]s of <math>A</math> with corresponding indices <math> n_1, \dots, n_s </math> (the index of an eigenvalue is the size of its largest [[Jordan normal form|Jordan block]]).{{sfn|Higham|2000|loc=Thm 1.3}}

==Matrix geometrical series==
Matrix polynomials can be used to sum a matrix geometrical series as one would an ordinary [[geometric series]],

:<math>S=I+A+A^2+\cdots +A^n</math>
:<math>AS=A+A^2+A^3+\cdots +A^{n+1}</math>
:<math>(I-A)S=S-AS=I-A^{n+1}</math>
:<math>S=(I-A)^{-1}(I-A^{n+1})</math>

If <math>I - A</math> is nonsingular one can evaluate the expression for the sum <math>S</math>.
